title: Nash Social Welfare for Multi Armed Bandits: Trajectory-wise Expected and High Probability Regret
claim: The stronger trajectory-wise metric is consistently larger than the ensemble metric, yet both shrink with more rounds and grow slowly with problem size.
layout: 3 line-plot panels in a row, shared two-series legend per panel
description: Three side-by-side line plots, each comparing two curves: a blue circle-marked line for Ensemble Nash Regret and an orange square-marked line for Trajectory-wise Nash Regret. The left panel plots regret against horizon T from 0 to 10000. Both curves decay steeply and then flatten, with the orange curve starting near 0.6 and staying above the blue one, which starts near 0.36. The center panel plots regret against the number of arms k from 5 to 50. Both curves rise roughly linearly, and the orange one climbs to about 0.34 while the blue one reaches about 0.17. The right panel plots regret against the worst arm mean from 0.12 to 0.40. The orange curve is nearly flat at about 0.10 to 0.11, and the blue curve rises slowly from about 0.065 to 0.08. Each panel has a legend in the top right and a light dashed grid. The eye goes first to the orange curve sitting above the blue one in every panel.
caption: Nash Regret comparisons. Left: Regret vs. horizon T. Center: Regret vs. number of arms k. Right: Regret vs. worst arm mean.
abstract: We study fair multi-armed bandits under the Nash Social Welfare (NSW) objective, which measures performance via the geometric mean of accumulated rewards. Existing work defines Nash regret as $\mathrm{NR}_T = Î¼^\star - (\prod_{t=1}^T \mathbb{E}Î¼_{I_t})^{1/T}$, where $Î¼_{I_t}$ is the mean reward of the recommended arm $I_t$ and $T$ is the horizon. Since it applies the geometric mean to per-round marginal expectations, it ignores the joint distribution of rewards across rounds, leaving the NSW fairness motivation unaddressed at the trajectory level. We propose \emph{trajectory-wise Nash regret} $\widetilde{\mathrm{NR}}_T = Î¼^\star - \mathbb{E}[(\prod_{t=1}^T Î¼_{I_t})^{1/T}]$, which computes the geometric mean over complete sample paths before taking expectations, capturing NSW fairness more faithfully. By Jensen's inequality, $\widetilde{\mathrm{NR}}_T \geq \mathrm{NR}_T$, making it a strictly stronger metric. We also introduce \emph{high probability Nash regret} $\widehat{\mathrm{NR}}_T = Î¼^\star - (\prod_t Î¼_{I_t})^{1/T}$, giving the first high probability regret bounds in fair bandits. Our two-phase algorithm, Round Robin Nash Confidence Bound (\texttt{RR-NCB}), combines round robin exploration with a Nash confidence bound index policy. We show $\widetilde{\mathrm{NR}}_T \leq \widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(\sqrt{k\log T/T})$ and, with probability $1-Î´$, $\widehat{\mathrm{NR}}_T \leq \widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(\sqrt{k\log(kT/Î´)/T})$, matching the optimal $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(\sqrt{k/T})$ rate despite the stronger metrics. Optimality follows from a lower bound via AM-GM and standard $k$-armed bandit minimax arguments. Simulations validate our theory.
